posts.content_md:
> **jean:** For those who use Vit. C developper, we know that this developper is very sensible to air and it oxyde rapidly.I find this :http://unblinkingeye.com/Articles/Preserv/preserv.htmlIs it a good way of preservation for the stock solution ?

That is a good article for interest. But I contend that the best way of dealing with ascorbate developer stock and it is a way we have been successfully using for some years in our labs is to "A and B" it. 

For A we have a 500ml bottle with:

20g ascorbic acid

3g Metol (4-methylaminophenol sulfate)

and top it up with 500ml deionized water

for B we have a 500 ml bottle of

50g sodium carbonate anhydrous

15g sodium hydroxide

top up with 500 ml deionized water.

(This one should be labeled "very caustic" )

Just use equal volumes of A and B from then on.

Now there are 3 bonus points for using Metol instead of phenidone.

1) is that phenidone is quite a strong silver halide solvent and tests have proved that metol gives brighter holograms.

2)The second point is that metol has a hardening action on gelatin and its effect on speeding up the development time over what you would have with just alkaline ascorbate means that even notoriously soft emulsions 

juch as PFG-03 can be in and out of the developer bath into a stop bath (~5% acetic acid ) in around 20 seconds, before the gelatin is seriously attacked. Assuming of course your exposure level was good enough.

3) Metol is a weaker reducing agent or developer than alkaline ascorbic acid.

When Metol gets oxidized it goes really dark brown so this is a useful indicator to tell you when your bath is exhausted because it wont go severely dark until most of the ascorbate has been oxidized. A mild yellowing like weak tea is quite OK . 

Dont forget to use the floating dish method of 2 closely fitting plastic dishes with the upper dish keeping most of the air out as it floats and acting as convenient agitator as well. 

Acid ascorbate in the stock soln A will not seriously oxidize for a year. 

(Slight yellowing is perfectly OK . )

jeff

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **MichaelH:** Yes, it's a rehalogenating bleach, EDTA.

OK that is the best type (DEwise) for Denisyuk reflection H's but not transmission ones.

So what happens with that type used WITHOUT FIXING in thiosulfate, is that the developed up silver gets re-oxidized to AgBr. But instead of returning you to square one and leaving you with a uniform coating and distribution of AgBr again just as it was before you exposed , it is energetically more favorable for the re-made AgBr to move over to the adjacent dark fringe made up of virgin AgBr and grow onto that dark fringe using the virgin AgBr grains as seeding centers. That actually requires the bleach solution to have some AgBr solvation ability to enable this carry over effect to occur. It has been found not to occur if the fringe spacing is too great as happens often with transmission Hs(ref. Hariharan). It also cannot happen if the bleach solution has no AgBr solvation ability such as with iodine-alcohol bleach. So the great thing about this carryover effect is that it theoretically uses all the original Ag in your emulsion to make the fringes whereas if you have to use fix you would have removed about half of your original silver content in the thiosulfate solution. The not good thing about it though is that the original 

sensitizing dyes become chemically locked into AgBr grains making the emulsion very vulnerable to print out. (This doesnt happen with dev-fix-bleach because the dyes get freed up and removed either in the fix or with the help of a bit of alcohol in the final rinse. This is convenient for transmission Hs where printout can be a more serious issue.) So from

all this one can say that provided your carry over bleach system has worked cleanly and left you with empty antinodes with all the silver migrated onto the adjacent nodes, then by using ascorbate you are gong to cause total printout of all that AgBr with its residual dyes. You can then re-bleach it. 

But it would be best to kill off those dyes so that they dont keep reforming absorption Hs instead of the more efficient phase Hs .

I found accidentally in a previous thread that pre-sensitizing BBplates with ascorbate mixed with Metol had a drastic effect of killing or inactivating those sensitizing dyes. This was found to be all due to Metol. So now we

could actually do with this dye killing effect! So that means putting metol in with your ascorbate(or just Metol alone would be fine) . Another sure fire way and probably the best is to kill off the dyes with dichromate soln.

But dont use dichromate as the second bleach as of course it is a reversal bleach and will remove the silver which is the last thing we want.

So I recommend doing the second bleach step again with ferric EDTA and then give it a good rinse in a dichromate bath. That will make it highly print-out resistant from then on. I hope I have not confused anyone with all this!

jeff

I think there's been indeed some confusion here about the nature of that ascorbate post-treatment. I understand it's been introduced by Phillips (*Bridging the gap between Soviet and western holography*, SPIE IS-8, 1990) to lower image noise by creating a thin layer of collloidal silver. That was mainly due to the lack of availability of ultra-fine grain emulsions back then. That technique mainly applied to 8E75 materials.

Incidentally, Michael, in that paper Phillips used 30g/L ascorbic acid.

I believe the printout issue with this kind of treatment has been brought up later by Saxby.

20g Ferric EDTA and 10 g KBr per litre. (This solution keeps for years.)

Resensitizing Bath

Then they are rinsed and immersed for 1 minute in a solution of: 

1% Ascorbic acid at pH ~6 (add sodium carbonate solution to get this pH)

The plates are then rinsed in deionized water and gently dried in a good air flow---all this has to be done in safelight conditions of course.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Wow, this is one of the best threads I have followed. Firstly I would like to say that the best printout prevention is very thorough rinsing! If you are not rinsing well none of the rest of this matters.

While printout can reduce the DE it also reduces the scattering so it is not always bad. Printout relaxation of dark stored holograms can also be a problem!

Jeff has a great idea of bleaching the final hologram to form silver iodine as it is the most stable form of silver. I have read of using 2.5g/l of potasium iodine. 

I have vague memories of a method of turning the silver to lead in order to make holograms more stable but I can't find the reference at the moment.

I also am greatly interested in Jeff's observation that development times must be kept low in order to keep the silver particles from growing into filaments. Does shortening the development time by heating the developer work the same as increasing the exposure time?

Acetic acid has been recomended by Bjelkhagen for a final rinse (10ml/l). It likely workes by removing the sensitizing dyes.

Chapter 8 of Bjelkhagen's Silver Halide Recording Materials is recomended reading for anyone who is trying to make thier holograms last longer. It has great tips such as laminating film to lexan and not to acrylic.

The post rpocessing that I use is to soak the plate in a 1% ascorbic acid solution for 30 seconds then turn on a 100w halogen light 1 foot from the plate for 5 minutes while the plate is still in the bath. This is intended to turn the un-exposed silver into colloidial silver. Then I give the plate a final 3 minute rinse.

This is intended to turn the un-exposed silver into colloidial silver. Then I give the plate a final 3 minute rinseThis is an interesting method.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** The post rpocessing that I use is to soak the plate in a 1% ascorbic acid solution for 30 seconds then turn on a 100w halogen light 1 foot from the plate for 5 minutes while the plate is still in the bath. This is intended to turn the un-exposed silver into colloidial silver. Then I give the plate a final 3 minute rinse.

That's actually Phillips' method.

Note, originally, Phillips advocated using a specially designed EDTA bleach, based on chloride instead of bromide (zinc chloride instead of potassium bromide).

Regarding the creation of a thin colloidal silver layer, of course the Russian GP developers may also be applied. By the way, I seem to remember we equally tried very diluted Neutol. So I assume a great many (diluted) developers might be successfully used.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
Colin and Jeff said:

> I also am greatly interested in Jeff's observation that development times must be kept low in order to keep the silver particles from growing into filaments. Does shortening the development time by heating the developer work the same as increasing the exposure time?This is an interesting key question Colin. My observation of some people years ago who had to make the brightest HIGs for a living with old Agfa film was that they used really warm (~30C) dev. with extra high alkalinity and very short dev times.~ 10 sec. after a lot of trial and error they found this gave the best results. So my gut feeling is that you do gain from warm dev and short dev time because fairly spheroidal grain growth is maximized. But electron micrographs need to prove this.

It reminds me of a time where for whatever reason I threw a fogged 60 cm square Agfa 8E75HD plate into the classic CWC2 brew with the room lights on. While watching the development I observed that the plate turned that colloidal red color in the first 10 seconds of immersion, and filed that info away for later experimenting, like exposing the heck out of a plate so that the time of development would only be 10" Still haven't followed up on it, but the next time I'm shooting SBR's I will try, because from the above quotes there seems that there could be an advantage to such a scheme!
